title: Queues and brokers: acknowledgements, redelivery and fan-out
goal: By the end you can explain why a broker sits between producers and consumers, route a message through an exchange, bindings and queues, predict what acknowledgements, prefetch and redelivery do to delivery and to per-key order, and choose between competing consumers and fan-out.

warmup.q: Your ledger service runs two instances on one RabbitMQ queue, with manual acks. For account acct-17 the queue holds m3 (auth 25) and then m4 (capture 25). Instance B takes m3 and crashes before acking it, while instance A is working on m4. In which order does the ledger book them?
options: m3, then m4: the queue is first in, first out, so processing is too
m4, then m3: m3 goes back to the queue and reaches A only after A has booked m4
Only m4: m3 was lost with instance B
m3, then m4: RabbitMQ puts m3 back at the head of the queue, ahead of m4
warmup.why: The broker keeps m3 until someone acks it, so nothing is lost: B's closed connection puts it back in the queue. It does go back to the head, which makes the last option tempting, but m4 left the queue before the crash and A books it first. The queue kept its order; the processing didn't. That is the reordering this lesson measures.

sections.h: Calling the consumers directly works until one of them is away
sections.body:
Your payment service authorizes about 1,200 card payments a second at peak, and three other services need to hear about every one: the ledger, the fraud check and the notification service. This track is about how that news travels. This lesson builds the classic answer, a message broker with queues. Lesson 2 builds the log, which is what Kafka is.

Any way of moving events from a **producer** (the service that has the news) to **consumers** (the services that need it) has to answer two questions. What happens when producers send faster than consumers can process? There are three choices: drop messages, buffer them, or slow the producer down, which is called **backpressure**. And what is lost when a machine crashes or a consumer goes away for a while?

The simplest design sends each event straight to each consumer. A **webhook** is the common form: every consumer registers a URL, and the producer sends an HTTP POST to it for each event. Market data feeds in finance use UDP multicast, one packet that reaches many receivers at once, for the lowest latency. Receivers spot gaps in the packets' sequence numbers and ask for the missing ones again, so the producer has to keep what it sent. ZeroMQ offers the same publish and subscribe pattern over TCP with no server in the middle. StatsD sends metrics over UDP and loses whatever doesn't arrive, which is fine for a request counter and wrong for money.

All of these assume both sides are up. Put numbers on it. The fraud check is down for a two-minute deploy. At 1,200 payments a second, the payment service must hold 144,000 events, about 140 MB at 1 KB each, and resend them later. If it drops them, the fraud check never sees two minutes of payments. If it keeps them in memory and then restarts itself, they are gone. And while the notification service needs 120 ms per call, a payment service that calls it inline waits 120 ms per payment.

So put a server in the middle whose only job is to hold messages: a **message broker**. The producer sends each event once and waits only for the broker to confirm that it has stored it. Consumers can be slow, restart or go away; their messages wait for them. The broker is a database specialized for this traffic, and it differs from an ordinary database in three ways. It deletes a message once a consumer has handled it, so it is no place to keep data. It assumes queues stay short, and its throughput drops once messages pile up and spill to disk. And instead of queries it offers subscriptions: a consumer says which messages it wants, and the broker pushes them as they arrive.

sections.h: A broker in the middle: exchanges, queues and bindings
sections.body:
AMQP 0-9-1, the protocol RabbitMQ grew up on, defines the broker's model as part of the protocol. It has three parts.

A **queue** holds messages in order until consumers take them. An **exchange** is where producers send messages. It stores nothing; it only decides which queues get a copy. A **binding** connects an exchange to a queue, optionally with a binding key. Every message carries a **routing key**, and the exchange's type says how routing keys and binding keys match:

| Exchange type | Puts a copy in |
|---|---|
| fanout | every bound queue, whatever the key |
| direct | each queue bound with a key equal to the routing key |
| topic | each queue whose binding pattern matches, such as `payments.*.eur` |
| headers | each queue whose header conditions match |

There is also a default exchange with an empty name, which routes a message to the queue named by its routing key.

Two patterns fall out of this. In **fan-out**, each service gets its own queue, bound to one exchange, so the ledger, the fraud check and the notifications each receive every payment. In **competing consumers**, several instances of one service read the same queue, and the broker gives each message to only one of them, which spreads the work. Most systems use both, as in the picture below: one queue per service, several instances per queue.

With the RabbitMQ Java client, the picture is a few calls:

```java
channel.exchangeDeclare("payments", BuiltinExchangeType.FANOUT, true);          // durable
channel.queueDeclare("ledger", true, false, false, Map.of("x-queue-type", "quorum"));
channel.queueBind("ledger", "payments", "");                                    // fanout ignores the key
channel.confirmSelect();                                                        // turn on publisher confirms
channel.basicPublish("payments", "", MessageProperties.PERSISTENT_TEXT_PLAIN, body);
channel.waitForConfirmsOrDie(5_000);                                            // stored, or an exception
```

```kotlin
channel.exchangeDeclare("payments", BuiltinExchangeType.FANOUT, true)           // durable
channel.queueDeclare("ledger", true, false, false, mapOf("x-queue-type" to "quorum"))
channel.queueBind("ledger", "payments", "")                                     // fanout ignores the key
channel.confirmSelect()                                                         // turn on publisher confirms
channel.basicPublish("payments", "", MessageProperties.PERSISTENT_TEXT_PLAIN, body)
channel.waitForConfirmsOrDie(5_000)                                             // stored, or an exception
```

The **publisher confirm** is the broker's receipt. For a quorum queue, RabbitMQ sends it once a majority of the queue's replicas have the message.

AMQP 1.0 is, despite the name, a different protocol. It defines how two peers move messages over links, with credit for flow control and outcomes such as accepted, released and rejected, and it leaves the broker model undefined. RabbitMQ 4.0 made 1.0 a core protocol that is always on, and maps addresses such as `/queues/ledger` or `/exchanges/payments` onto the same exchanges and queues. JMS, now Jakarta Messaging, is a Java API, not a wire protocol: queues for competing consumers, topics for fan-out. Apache ActiveMQ Artemis implements it, and became an Apache top-level project of its own in late 2025.

try.title: One publish, three copies
steps: From the `labs` folder, start RabbitMQ 4.4: `docker compose -f env/rabbitmq.yml up -d --wait`. It is ready in a few seconds and is capped at 512 MB. Then open a shell in it: `docker compose -f env/rabbitmq.yml exec rabbitmq bash`.
Run the block below. It declares a fanout exchange `payments` and three quorum queues bound to it, publishes one payment, and takes one message from each queue.
Before you run it: what will the second `get` on `ledger` return, and does it change what `notify` has?
Keep the shell open for the next Try-its.

code.title: inside the rabbitmq container
code.src:
# inside the rabbitmq container
rabbitmqadmin declare exchange --name payments --type fanout --durable true
for q in ledger fraud-check notify; do
  rabbitmqadmin declare queue --name $q --type quorum --durable true
  rabbitmqadmin declare binding --source payments --destination-type queue --destination $q --routing-key ""
done
rabbitmqadmin publish message --exchange payments --routing-key "" --payload 'auth acct-17 40.00 EUR'

echo "== ledger";        rabbitmqadmin get messages --queue ledger --table-style borderless
echo "== fraud-check";   rabbitmqadmin get messages --queue fraud-check --table-style borderless
echo "== ledger again";  rabbitmqadmin get messages --queue ledger --table-style borderless
echo "== notify";        rabbitmqadmin get messages --queue notify --table-style borderless

try.expect:
Columns trimmed (`payload_bytes`, `exchange`, `properties` and `payload_encoding` left out):
```text
Message published and routed successfully
== ledger
 redelivered   routing_key   message_count   payload
 false                       0               auth acct-17 40.00 EUR
== fraud-check
 redelivered   routing_key   message_count   payload
 false                       0               auth acct-17 40.00 EUR
== ledger again
 redelivered   routing_key   message_count   payload
== notify
 redelivered   routing_key   message_count   payload
 false                       0               auth acct-17 40.00 EUR
```
One publish, three copies: the fanout exchange put one in each bound queue. `get` acknowledged the ledger's copy (its default ack mode, `ack_requeue_false`, means "ack, don't requeue"), so the second get on `ledger` came back empty, while `notify` still had its own copy. `message_count` is how many messages were left in that queue after the get. `rabbitmqadmin get` polls through the HTTP API and is for experiments only; a real service subscribes with `basicConsume`.

sections.h: Acknowledgements and redelivery, and the reordering they cause
sections.body:
A broker must not delete a message just because it sent it: the consumer may crash halfway through. So the consumer **acknowledges** each message (acks it) once it has finished, and only then does the broker delete it. A message that was delivered and not yet acked is **unacked**: it stays in the queue, reserved for that consumer.

If the consumer's connection closes before the ack, because the process crashed or the network dropped, RabbitMQ puts every unacked delivery back in the queue, at its original position when it can, and delivers it again with the `redeliver` flag set. That is **redelivery**. It gives you at-least-once delivery: no message is lost, and some are processed twice. The common case is a consumer that booked a payment and died before its ack left. The broker can't tell that apart from a consumer that died before it started, so it sends the message again, and the consumer has to recognize the repeat. The worked example builds that.

You can switch acks off. With **auto-ack** the broker counts a message as acknowledged the moment it sends it. RabbitMQ's documentation calls that mode unsafe: a consumer that crashes loses every message it held, which is at-most-once delivery.

Most consumers should look like this:

```java
channel.basicQos(100);                                          // prefetch: the next section
channel.basicConsume("ledger", false, (consumerTag, d) -> {      // false: manual acks
    book(d.getBody());
    channel.basicAck(d.getEnvelope().getDeliveryTag(), false);  // ack only after the work is done
}, consumerTag -> {});
```

```kotlin
channel.basicQos(100)                                           // prefetch: the next section
channel.basicConsume("ledger", false, DeliverCallback { _, d ->  // false: manual acks
    book(d.body)
    channel.basicAck(d.envelope.deliveryTag, false)             // ack only after the work is done
}, CancelCallback { })
```

Redelivery has a cost few people expect: it reorders. A queue is first in, first out at the moment it hands messages out, and only there. Step through it below: two consumers share a queue, five events of one account arrive, and one consumer crashes. RabbitMQ puts m3 back at the head of the queue, but by then m4 has already left it, and the ledger books a capture before its authorization. AMQP and JMS both promise that a queue keeps its order, and this queue does. The processing order doesn't, and the ledger only sees the processing order. Inside a broker the fix is one consumer per queue (RabbitMQ's single active consumer), which gives up competing consumers. Lessons 2 and 3 show how a log gets order and parallel consumers at once.

steps: In the container shell, run the block below. `--ack-mode reject_requeue_true` takes a message and hands it back unacked, which is what happens to a crashed consumer's deliveries.

rabbitmqadmin declare queue --name captures --type quorum --durable true
for m in m1 m2 m3; do rabbitmqadmin publish message --routing-key captures --payload "$m capture acct-17"; done

echo "== take one, give it back unacked"

Columns trimmed:
```text
== take one, give it back unacked
 redelivered   message_count   properties                                             payload
 false         2                                                                      m1 capture acct-17
== take the next one
 redelivered   message_count   properties                                             payload
 true          2               headers: {"x-acquired-count":1,"x-delivery-count":1}   m1 capture acct-17
== take three and ack them
 redelivered   message_count   properties                                             payload

```
The "next" message was m1 again: a returned message goes back to its original position, the head, ahead of m2. Its second delivery says `redelivered: true`, and the quorum queue counts the returns in `x-delivery-count`. `x-acquired-count`, new in RabbitMQ 4.3, counts every time a consumer took the message. A crashed consumer's unacked deliveries come back exactly like this; the difference is only that a whole batch returns at once.

refs.title: RabbitMQ: consumer acknowledgements and publisher confirms

sections.h: Prefetch and backpressure: how much a consumer may hold
sections.body:
A consumer that asked for one message, processed it, acked it and only then asked for the next would wait a network round trip after every message. With 2 ms of work and a 1 ms round trip, that is 3 ms per message: 333 a second instead of 500. So brokers push messages ahead of time, and **prefetch** caps how many unacked deliveries one consumer may hold. In AMQP the setting is `basic.qos`. RabbitMQ's docs say values from 100 to 300 usually give the best throughput, and quorum queues cap a consumer's prefetch at 2,000.

A bigger prefetch is not free. Every message a consumer holds is one more message that comes back if it crashes, and one more that a sibling can overtake. A consumer that holds 1,000 messages and works through them slowly also leaves its siblings idle, because the broker has already promised those messages to it. And auto-ack has no prefetch at all: the broker sends as fast as the socket takes it. The Try-it below measures all of this on a model of the queue.

Prefetch is one form of backpressure: the consumer says "no more until I ack". Every hop between producer and consumer needs one, and you have met the first of these already.

- TCP has it built in. A receiver that stops reading shrinks its window to zero and the sender's writes block (the Networking track's lesson on TCP windows).
- RabbitMQ pushes back on producers too. When a node runs low on memory or disk, it stops reading from publishing connections. A queue with a length limit and `overflow=reject-publish` refuses new messages, which the producer sees as a negative publisher confirm.
- NATS JetStream stops sending to a consumer at `MaxAckPending` unacknowledged messages, 1,000 by default.
- In Amazon SQS a received message turns invisible for its visibility timeout, 30 seconds by default and at most 12 hours, and becomes visible again if the consumer doesn't delete it in time. Deleting is SQS's ack. A standard queue allows about 120,000 messages in flight.

A log buffers in a different way. Lesson 2 shows that it keeps every message on disk until retention removes it, so a slow consumer only falls behind and slows down nobody else.

try.title: Measure duplicates, inversions and losses
steps: Run the demo from the `labs` folder (command below; no Docker needed). It pushes 1,000 payment events for 10 accounts through an in-memory model of a queue: consumers need 1 to 3 ticks per message, and the crashing consumer dies every 25 ticks just after finishing a message and before its ack.
Predict first. With one consumer that crashes, will any account's events be booked out of order? With two consumers and no crash at all?
Look at the `2 consumers, prefetch 1` row. Why does it have duplicates but no inversions? (Hint: with 10 accounts published in turn, which messages are in flight at the same time?)
Run it again with `-Pargs=10` for a crash every 10 ticks, and compare the auto-ack row.

```text
1,000 payments, 10 accounts; a crash every 25 ticks
setup                                  booked redelivered duplicates inversions  lost
1 consumer,  prefetch 10, no crash       1000           0          0          0     0
1 consumer,  prefetch 10, crashes        1109        1096        109          0     0
2 consumers, prefetch 1,  crashes        1044          44         44          0     0
2 consumers, prefetch 10, no crash       1000           0          0         35     0
2 consumers, prefetch 10, crashes        1021         417         21        131     0
2 consumers, prefetch 100, crashes       1025        3808         25        357     0
1 consumer,  auto-ack, crashes            541           0          0          0   459
2 queues by account, 1 consumer each     1108        1081        108          0     0
```
The model has no randomness, so you get exactly these numbers, and the Java and Kotlin versions print the same table. One consumer never reorders: returned messages go back to the head and it takes them again in order, so crashes only cost duplicates (one per crash, the message whose ack was lost). Two consumers reorder 35 events even with no crash, because two of one account's events can be in flight at once and the second can finish first; crashes raise that to 131, and prefetch 100 to 357, with nearly 4,000 redeliveries. With prefetch 1 only two neighbouring events are ever in flight, and neighbours belong to different accounts, so nothing is reordered. Auto-ack lost 459 of 1,000 payments. With `-Pargs=10` the duplicates and losses roughly triple.

sections.h: Poison messages, dead letters, and what a log does differently
sections.body:
Some messages can never succeed. A settlement event arrives with `"amount": "forty"`, the parser throws, and the consumer crashes before its ack. The broker redelivers the message to the next consumer, which crashes too. With competing consumers, one bad message takes down every instance in turn while the rest of the queue waits. This is a **poison message**.

The defence is a **delivery limit**: count how often a message came back, and stop redelivering it after N returns. Since RabbitMQ 4.0, quorum queues stop at 20 returns by default, and consumers see the count in the `x-delivery-count` header. Over the limit, the queue drops the message, or moves it to a **dead-letter queue** (DLQ) if the queue has a dead-letter exchange. Treat every message in a DLQ as an incident: someone has to find the cause, fix it and replay the message, or decide it is safe to throw away.

A DLQ is not lossless by default. Quorum queues dead-letter **at-most-once**: if the dead-letter target can't take the message, it is gone, with no error anywhere. At-least-once dead-lettering has to be switched on: `dead-letter-strategy=at-least-once` together with `overflow=reject-publish` on the source queue.

Here is how the products you are likely to meet line up:

| Product (November 2026) | Competing consumers | Fan-out | Poison messages |
|---|---|---|---|
| RabbitMQ 4.4 | several consumers on one queue | an exchange bound to one queue per service | delivery limit (20), then a dead-letter exchange |
| Apache Artemis (JMS) | a JMS queue, or a shared topic subscription | a JMS topic | a redelivery limit, then a dead-letter address |
| Amazon SQS and SNS | consumers polling one SQS queue | an SNS topic delivering to one SQS queue per service | a redrive policy: after `maxReceiveCount` receives, the DLQ |
| NATS JetStream | several workers on one pull consumer | one consumer per service on a stream | `MaxDeliver` caps redeliveries |

RabbitMQ's quorum queues are the default choice for a replicated queue: each is a Raft group, with three replicas by default (the Consistency and consensus track built Raft). RabbitMQ 4.0 removed the older mirrored classic queues, 4.3 added 32 strict priorities and consumer timeouts, and 4.4.0 (October 2026) added delayed messages.

Look at what every broker here keeps: a state per message (ready, unacked, delivered to whom, returned how often), and nothing once the message is acked. That makes sharing work message by message easy, and it costs three things you have now seen. A new service can't read last week's payments, because they are gone. You can't replay a day after a bug. And competing consumers lose per-account order. Lesson 2 keeps every message in an append-only log and lets each reader keep one number, its position. The Try-it table's last row previews how a log gets order back: one queue per group of accounts, each with a single consumer, kept every account in order.

try.title: Watch a poison message reach the dead-letter queue
steps: In the container shell, run the block below. It makes a quorum queue `settlements` with a delivery limit of 3 and a dead-letter queue, publishes a settlement whose amount can't be parsed, and fails on it again and again.
Predict: on which attempt does the queue stop delivering it, and what will `x-delivery-count` say in the dead-letter queue?
Exit the shell and stop RabbitMQ from the `labs` folder: `docker compose -f env/rabbitmq.yml down -v`.

code.src:

rabbitmqadmin declare queue --name settlements --type quorum --durable true \

  echo "== attempt $i"

try.expect:
Columns trimmed:
```text
== attempt 1
 redelivered   properties                                             payload
 false                                                                {"merchant": "m-881", "amount": "forty"}
== attempt 2
 true          headers: {"x-acquired-count":1,"x-delivery-count":1}   {"merchant": "m-881", "amount": "forty"}
== attempt 3
 true          headers: {"x-acquired-count":2,"x-delivery-count":2}   {"merchant": "m-881", "amount": "forty"}
== attempt 4
 true          headers: {"x-acquired-count":3,"x-delivery-count":3}   {"merchant": "m-881", "amount": "forty"}
== attempt 5
 redelivered   properties   payload
== the dead-letter queue
 true          headers: {"x-acquired-count":4,"x-death":[{"count":1,"exchange":"","queue":"settlements",
               "reason":"delivery_limit",...}],"x-delivery-count":4,...}   {"merchant": "m-881", "amount": "forty"}
```
Four deliveries, then the queue stopped trying: the fourth return took `x-delivery-count` past the limit of 3, and the message moved to `settlements.dlq` with an `x-death` header that says where it came from and why (`delivery_limit`). With the default limit of 20 and no dead-letter exchange, the same loop delivers the message 21 times and then deletes it.

analogy: A broker queue works like the ticket rail in a restaurant kitchen. Orders arrive on tickets and clip onto the rail in order. A cook takes the next ticket, and it stays clipped above that cook's station until the dish goes out (the ack); only then is it thrown away. If a cook walks out mid-dish, the ticket goes back to the front of the rail, but the cook at the next station may already be plating the following course for the same table. Fan-out is a copy of every ticket for the bar and one for the kitchen. The analogy breaks at durability and at knowledge: a real broker writes each ticket to disk on several machines before it says thanks, and it never knows whether a dish was cooked, only whether someone said so.
in_your_world: Plenty of payment platforms run RabbitMQ, SQS or an IBM MQ next to Kafka, often for notifications, webhooks to merchants and work queues. The defaults decide your failure modes, so set them on purpose: manual acks, sent only after the database commit; a prefetch you chose (start near 100); quorum queues with a dead-letter exchange; and an alert on DLQ depth, since every dead letter is a payment someone must look at. Keep competing consumers away from anything that must stay in order per account, such as ledger postings or a payment's state changes. Use single active consumer, one queue per group of accounts, or a Kafka topic keyed by account. And since every queue in this lesson delivers at least once, give each event an idempotency key and let the consumer drop repeats, whether it runs in a Quarkus service or inside a Temporal activity.
mistake: Scaling a consumer by adding instances on the same queue and assuming the queue's order still holds. A team's ledger consumer falls behind, so they run four instances instead of one. Throughput quadruples, and every few days a capture is booked before its authorization: two events of one account were in flight on two instances, or one came back after a crash. Nothing logs an error, because each instance did exactly what it was told. People make this mistake because "the queue is FIFO" is true and sounds like a promise about processing. The fix is to decide which order you need before you scale: per-account order needs one consumer per account's queue (single active consumer, or several queues split by account), or a log partitioned by account, as lesson 3 of this track shows. Work with no order requirement, such as sending receipts, can scale with competing consumers freely.

kotlin.title: Kotlin

compare.note: Both lean on `Message` being a Kotlin data class: `equals` and `hashCode` compare key and seq, so a `HashSet` spots a repeat. `seen.add(m)` returns false when the element was already there, which makes the duplicate test one call in both languages. Java reads the properties through getters (`m.getKey()`), Kotlin by name (`m.key`). Kotlin's `highest[m.key]` returns `Int?`, and the `top != null` check smart-casts it to `Int` for the comparison; Java's `Integer top` would throw a `NullPointerException` if you compared it unboxed without the null check. In Kotlin `if ... else` is an expression, so the update fits on one line.

worked.title: Make a redelivered payment harmless: dedupe, commit, then ack

steps.say: The ledger consumer will see some payments twice: every crash between booking and ack causes one. So the producer gives each event a unique id when it creates it (an idempotency key), and the consumer remembers which ids it has booked. Start by reading the id from the message. (`Event` is your own parsed type; `channel` is the consumer's RabbitMQ channel.)

Record the id and book the payment in one database transaction. `processed_events` has the event id as its primary key, so a second insert of the same id changes nothing, and `executeUpdate` returns 0. Book only when the insert returned 1. (PostgreSQL syntax; in Oracle use `MERGE` or catch the unique-key error.)

Ack only after the commit. If the process dies between commit and ack, the broker redelivers, the insert finds the id, nothing is booked twice, and this time the ack goes out. If the transaction itself fails, hand the message back with `basicReject(tag, true)`; on a quorum queue that counts towards the delivery limit, so a payment that always fails ends in the DLQ instead of looping.

Why not just skip messages whose `redeliver` flag is set? Because the flag means "may have been seen", in both directions. A redelivered message may never have been booked (the consumer died before starting), so skipping it loses a payment. And a repeat can arrive with the flag unset: a producer whose publisher confirm got lost publishes the event again, and the broker sees two separate messages. Only the id tells you for sure. The Encoding track's lesson on calling other services made a retried request safe with the same idea.

lab.title: Build a broker queue, then measure what redelivery does to order
steps: Run the tests from the `labs` folder. All 27 fail: the stubs throw `NotImplementedError` or `UnsupportedOperationException`. No Docker needed; the whole lab runs in a second or two.

In `MiniQueue.kt`, write `deliver`: look up the subscription (missing means `IllegalStateException`), return null at the prefetch limit unless the consumer uses auto-ack, take the head of `waiting`, remember it in `inFlight` (not for auto-ack), and build the `Delivery`.

Write `ack`, then `giveBack`, `reject` and `disconnect`. A returned message keeps its `position`, so putting it back in the `TreeMap` puts it back at the head. Count the return first, and dead-letter it once the count passes `deliveryLimit`.
In `OrderCheck.java`, write `check` as its javadoc says. In `Exchange.java`, write `route` and `publish`.

Run the tests until all 27 pass. `MiniQueueTest` includes the five-message stepper as a test. `RedeliveryTest` runs 1,000 payments through your queue with `ConsumerSim` (in the test folder) and checks the shape of the Try-it's table: no inversions with one consumer, some with two, more with crashes and a big prefetch, losses with auto-ack, none with one queue per group of accounts.
hints: `waiting.pollFirstEntry()?.value` takes the head of the queue, or null when it is empty. `inFlight.remove(tag) ?: throw IllegalStateException(...)` removes and checks in one line.

In `disconnect`, copy the tags first (`inFlight.filterValues { it.consumer == consumer }.keys.toList()`): removing entries from a map while you iterate over it throws `ConcurrentModificationException`.

`Message` is a Kotlin data class, so Java calls `m.getKey()` and `m.getSeq()`, and a `HashSet<Message>` compares key and seq. In `Exchange.route`, `targets.contains(queue)` keeps a queue that is bound twice from getting two copies.

drill.title: Trace two consumers from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking back: one queue holds m1 to m5 for account acct-17. Consumers A and B have prefetch 2 and manual acks. A takes m1 and m2; B takes m3 and m4. A books m1 and acks it. B books m3 and crashes before its ack leaves. A books m2 and acks it, then takes whatever is next, and from then on A handles everything. Write down the order in which the ledger books messages, then count duplicates and inversions the way the lab's `OrderCheck` does.

answer.src:
booked: m1 (A), m3 (B), m2 (A), m3 (A, redelivered), m4 (A, redelivered), m5 (A)

B's crash returns m3 and m4 to the head of the queue, in their old order.
A's next two deliveries are m3 and m4, both with redeliver=true; then m5.

duplicates: 1   m3 was booked by B and again by A (B's ack was lost)
inversions: 1   m2 was booked after m3, before any redelivery: two consumers in parallel
                are enough to reorder. m4 and m5 are in order.

recap: Sending events straight to consumers (webhooks, UDP multicast, ZeroMQ) assumes both sides are up; a broker in the middle stores messages until consumers take them.

In AMQP 0-9-1, producers publish to an exchange, bindings decide which queues get a copy, and consumers read queues. One queue per service gives fan-out; several consumers on one queue are competing consumers.
A broker deletes a message only when it is acked. Unacked deliveries of a closed connection are redelivered with `redeliver=true`, which gives at-least-once delivery; auto-ack gives at-most-once.
Queues are FIFO when they hand messages out, not when consumers finish them. Competing consumers reorder an account's events, and redelivery and a large prefetch reorder them more.
Prefetch caps unacked deliveries per consumer (100 to 300 is typical); it is the consumer's backpressure, and a larger value means more redelivered on a crash.
A delivery limit (20 on RabbitMQ quorum queues since 4.0) stops poison messages, and a dead-letter queue keeps them, at-most-once unless you configure at-least-once.

quiz.q: A notification consumer uses auto-ack with a large prefetch for speed. It has received 40 messages and processed 12 when its pod is killed. What happens to the other 28?
options: They are redelivered to another consumer with `redeliver=true`
They return to the head of the queue in their original order
They are lost: with auto-ack the broker deleted each one as it sent it
They go to the dead-letter queue because their delivery failed
quiz.why: Auto-ack tells the broker to count a message as acknowledged the moment it leaves, so there is nothing left to redeliver. That is at-most-once delivery, which is why RabbitMQ calls the mode unsafe. The first two options describe manual acks, where unacked deliveries do come back.

quiz.q: Payments flow through a fanout exchange to one queue per service. A new `chargeback-alerts` service binds a new queue today and wants last week's payments too. What does it get?
options: Only payments published after its queue was bound: earlier ones were acked and deleted from the other queues
Last week's payments, copied over from the ledger queue
Everything still in any queue, because the exchange keeps a history
Last week's payments, as long as the queues are quorum queues
quiz.why: An exchange stores nothing and a queue deletes what it has delivered and seen acked. A queue that didn't exist when a message was published never got a copy. Getting history needs something that keeps messages after they are read, which is the log of the next lesson.

quiz.q: A fraud-check consumer has prefetch 2,000 and takes 50 ms per message. Its sibling on the same queue is idle, and when the busy one crashes, a flood of redeliveries follows. What change helps most?
options: Switch to auto-ack so the broker stops tracking deliveries
Move the queue to a fanout exchange
Raise the delivery limit
Lower the prefetch, so each consumer holds a few hundred at most and the rest stay in the queue for whoever is free
quiz.why: Prefetch is how many unacked messages one consumer may hold. At 2,000 and 50 ms each, one consumer is promised 100 seconds of work while its sibling waits, and a crash returns up to 2,000 messages at once. A smaller prefetch spreads the work and shrinks what a crash returns. Auto-ack would lose messages instead.

quiz.q: The runbook says: "Nothing is ever lost; failed settlements end up in the DLQ." The `settlements` quorum queue uses the default settings plus a dead-letter exchange. Which statement is right?
options: The runbook is right: dead-lettering always retries until the DLQ has the message
Quorum queues dead-letter at-most-once by default: a dead letter the target can't take is lost; at-least-once needs `dead-letter-strategy=at-least-once` and `overflow=reject-publish`
Quorum queues can't dead-letter at all; only classic queues can
Messages over the delivery limit are never removed, so nothing can be lost
quiz.why: At-most-once is the quorum queues' default dead-letter strategy, so a DLQ that is full, missing or unreachable means the message disappears without an error. The last option ignores that the delivery limit (20 by default) removes messages from the source queue.

quiz.q: Ledger postings must be booked in order per account, and one consumer instance can't keep up. Which design gives you two instances and keeps per-account order through crashes?
options: Two competing consumers on one queue with prefetch 1
Two competing consumers on one quorum queue, because Raft keeps the order
Two queues, with each account routed to one of them by a direct exchange, and one consumer per queue
Two consumers with auto-ack, so nothing is ever redelivered out of order
quiz.why: Order survives only if each account's events have one reader at a time. Routing by account into two queues with one consumer each does that, and the lab measures zero inversions with it. Prefetch 1 makes reordering rarer but not impossible: two events of one account can still be in flight on two instances, as in the stepper. Raft orders the queue's log, not the consumers' processing.

flashcards.front: What do an exchange, a binding and a queue each do in AMQP 0-9-1?
flashcards.back: The exchange receives published messages and stores nothing. Bindings say which queues get a copy. The queue holds messages in order until consumers take and ack them.

flashcards.front: Fan-out or competing consumers: which is one queue per service, and which is several consumers on one queue?
flashcards.back: Fan-out is one queue per service, each getting every message. Competing consumers share one queue, and each message goes to only one of them.

flashcards.front: What happens to unacked deliveries when a RabbitMQ consumer's connection closes?
flashcards.back: They are requeued, at their original position when possible, and redelivered with the `redeliver` flag set to true.

flashcards.front: Why does a FIFO queue with two consumers still reorder messages?
flashcards.back: Order holds when the queue hands messages out. Two consumers finish at their own pace, and a redelivered message reaches a consumer after later messages have already been processed.
How many unacknowledged deliveries one consumer may hold. RabbitMQ suggests 100 to 300; auto-ack has no limit.

flashcards.front: What is the default delivery limit of a RabbitMQ quorum queue, and what happens past it?
flashcards.back: 20, since RabbitMQ 4.0. Past it the message is dropped, or dead-lettered if the queue has a dead-letter exchange.

flashcards.front: Is dead-lettering on RabbitMQ quorum queues lossless by default?
flashcards.back: No. The default strategy is at-most-once. At-least-once needs `dead-letter-strategy=at-least-once` and `overflow=reject-publish`.

terms.plain: A server between producers and consumers that stores messages until consumers have handled them.
The AMQP object producers publish to. It stores nothing and copies each message into the queues whose bindings match.
A consumer's signal that it has finished a message. Only then does the broker delete it.
The broker delivering a message again because its consumer disconnected or rejected it before acking.
Several consumers on one queue; each message goes to one of them.
Every subscriber gets every message, usually through one queue per subscriber.
The most unacknowledged deliveries one consumer may hold at a time.
A queue that collects messages that failed too often or were rejected, for a person to inspect.

explain_back.prompt: A colleague says: "We use a FIFO queue with manual acks, so our four ledger instances book every account's payments exactly once and in order." Explain which parts of that are true and what you would change.
explain_back.answer: Manual acks mean no payment is lost: the broker keeps a message until someone acks it, and gives it back if a consumer dies first. But that is at-least-once, not exactly once. A consumer that books a payment and dies before its ack gets the payment redelivered to another instance, so the ledger needs an idempotency key per event and must skip ids it has already booked, in the same transaction as the booking. The order claim is false too. The queue hands messages out in order, but four instances finish at their own pace, and a redelivered message arrives after later ones were already booked. For per-account order I'd stop sharing one queue: route accounts into several queues with one consumer each, or use single active consumer, or use a Kafka topic keyed by account, where each partition has one reader per group.

deeper.body:
**AMQP 1.0's flow control.** In 1.0 a receiver grants a sender **link credit**: a number of messages it may send. Credit is prefetch made explicit and per link, and a receiver can stop a sender by granting none. Each transfer then settles with an outcome. RabbitMQ maps `accepted` to an ack, `released` to a requeue and `rejected` to dead-lettering or a drop, and supports `modified` on quorum queues. RabbitMQ 4.0 made 1.0 a core protocol and reported more than double the peak throughput of 3.13 on some workloads.

**Two counters since RabbitMQ 4.3.** Quorum queues now keep `acquired-count`, raised every time a message is returned for any reason, and `delivery-count`, raised only when a delivery failed. A client crash and `basic.reject` count as failures; according to the 4.3 release blog, a `basic.nack` and a consumer timeout raise only the acquired count. The delivery limit checks `delivery-count`, so a consumer that hands messages back without marking them failed can do so without limit.

**Comparing brokers fairly.** The 2011 Kafka paper (Kreps, Narkhede and Rao) measured about 400,000 messages a second from one producer sending batches of 50, against far less for ActiveMQ and RabbitMQ of the time. Its own authors note that the Kafka producer didn't wait for the broker's acknowledgement, while the other brokers tracked the delivery state of every message. A benchmark between systems means something only at equal guarantees.

**Brokers keep moving.** NATS Server 2.12 added atomic batch publish to JetStream: the batch commits only if every message in it passes the stream's checks. RabbitMQ streams are an append-only log inside RabbitMQ with non-destructive reads, the same idea as the next lesson. And Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition, chapter 12, frames this whole lesson around the two questions of section 1: what happens when producers outrun consumers, and what is lost in a crash.
